extracted.intended_audience: military legal officers, judge advocates, courts-martial, convening authorities
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for admissibility of evidence, evaluation of witnesses, and proper form/content of findings and specifications in courts-martial proceedings under the Articles of War. Covers documentary authentication, impeachment, prior convictions for punishment, permissible substitutions in findings, and defenses to specific charges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Witness credibility assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: It IS an important part of the judgment of the court, in a case where the evidence is conflicting, to determine the measure of the credibility to be attached to the several witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In its finding the court may, in connection with the testimony, properly take into consideration the appearance and deportment of the witnesses on the stand and their manner of testifying, especially when under cross-examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight of official records
rubrics_metrics.description: Official records are of a high class of evidence as to the facts which are recorded in them pursuant to the special objects for which they are kept, but they have not this weight as evidence with reference to other facts incidentally recorded in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Muster-in rolls are primary evidence of the dates of muster in as muster-out rolls are of the dates of muster out; they cannot be used to impeach the muster-in as fixed by the muster-in roll. Entries are subject to rebuttal by proof of mistake or fraud, and entries are not proof of commission of an offense (e.g., desertion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentication and admissibility of bureau-authenticated copies
rubrics_metrics.description: War Department Orders of May 15, 1894...provide that 'official copies of orders and other papers shall be authenticated solely by an impressed seal of the bureau issuing the same' — intended for administrative use, not as evidence before civil courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copies so authenticated would not be admissible as evidence in civil courts; before courts-martial such copies, authenticated by the official stamp of the bureau, in the absence of objection, would be legally admissible; the Secretary of War could by regulation provide acceptance in courts-martial notwithstanding objection of the accused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original official documents as competent evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The enlistment paper, the physical examination paper, and the outline card are original writings made by officers in the performance of duty and are competent evidence of the facts recited therein.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copies authenticated under the seal of the War Department, according to section 882, R.S., are equally admissible with the originals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copies of courts-martial records
rubrics_metrics.description: Copies of records of courts-martial authenticated under the seal of the War Department, as provided by section 882, R.S., are admissible in evidence 'equally with the originals.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authentication under the proper statute/regulation required for parity with originals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copies of title-affecting papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers which contain evidence of title, such as deeds, conveyances, etc., by which the United States holds lands, and which are on file in the War Department, may be proven by copies, as provided by section 882, R.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certified copies admitted equally with originals for proving title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Muster rolls as evidence (rebuttable)
rubrics_metrics.description: The muster rolls on file in the War Department are official records and copies of the same, duly certified, are evidence of the facts originally entered therein and not compiled from other sources — subject of course to be rebutted by proper evidence that they are mistaken or incorrect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though evidence that a soldier was duly enlisted or mustered into service, they may be rebutted by proof of fraud or illegality in the enlistment or muster, properly invalidating the proceeding and entitling the soldier to a discharge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of muster roll extracts to prove absence/desertion
rubrics_metrics.description: Absence without leave of a soldier may be shown by extracts from the muster rolls, covering the period of absence, authenticated in the manner specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the entry states desertion, it is evidence of absence without leave; intent remains for court determination in light of all facts and circumstances. Extended unexplained absence plus apprehension in civilian clothes at a distant point may justify conviction of desertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compiled statements inadmissible
rubrics_metrics.description: A compiled statement is not admissible as evidence before courts-martial, as it is not a copy of an original record, but simply a statement of what is therein contained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authentication by the impressed stamp 'official copy' of the bureau or office having custody of the original would be improper for a compiled statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving general and special orders
rubrics_metrics.description: General orders issued from the War Department or Headquarters of the Army may ordinarily be proven by printed official copies in the usual form; the court will in general properly take judicial notice of the printed order as genuine and correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A court-martial, however, should not, in general, accept in evidence, if objected to, a printed or written special order which has not been made public to the Army, without some proof of its genuineness and official character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility procedure for Morning Report Book extracts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Morning Report Book is an original writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To properly admit extracts in evidence, the book should be first identified by the proper custodian, and the extracts then not merely read to the court by the witness, but copied and the copies, properly verified, attached as exhibits to the record of the court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility of duplicates when originals unavailable
rubrics_metrics.description: Copies of pay accounts (charged to have been duplicated) are admissible in evidence where the accused has by his own act placed the originals beyond the reach of process, and fails to produce them in court on proper notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similarly admissible where originals are in hands of a person who has left the United States so they cannot be reached, after notice to the accused to produce or otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive lists as secondary evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A descriptive list is but secondary evidence and not admissible to prove the facts recited therein.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not a record of original entries made by an officer under a duty imposed upon him by law or the custom of the service, but is simply a compilation of facts taken from other records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of handwriting for contested writings
rubrics_metrics.description: To the admission in evidence of a letter written and signed by the accused (of which the introduction is contested), proof of his handwriting is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of handwriting by comparison is not admissible at common law except where the standard of comparison is an acknowledged or proved genuine writing already in evidence in the case. A writing not in evidence simply offered as a standard is not admissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility of telegraphic company copies and operator testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: The written or printed copy furnished by the telegraph company and received by the person to whom it is addressed should in general be admitted in evidence by a court-martial in the absence of circumstances casting a reasonable doubt upon its genuineness or correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where it is necessary to prove that a telegram which was not received, or the receipt of which is denied and not proven, was actually duly sent, the operator or proper official of the company, or other person cognizant of the fact of sending, should be summoned as a witness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inadmissibility of ex parte affidavits
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits, taken ex parte, and not as depositions under article 91, are in no case admissible as evidence on a trial by court-martial, if objected to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such affidavits are excluded when properly objected to by opposing counsel/accused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of accused's repeated false statements in embezzlement cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated false statements of the accused relative to the public moneys for which he was accountable are competent evidence going to sustain a charge of embezzlement under article 60.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: False statements may be used substantively to show culpability with respect to accountability for public funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding should conform to plea in absence of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Where no evidence is introduced, the general rule is that the finding should conform to the plea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the accused pleads guilty or not guilty and there is no evidence, the verdict should match the plea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency between charge and specification findings
rubrics_metrics.description: The finding on the charge should be supported by the finding on the specification (or specifications), and the two findings should be consistent with each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A finding of guilty on the charge would be quite inconsistent with a finding of not guilty, or guilty without attaching criminality, on the specification. No matter how many specifications there may be, it requires a finding of guilty or not guilty on but one specification (apposite to the charge) to support a similar finding upon the charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot acquit specification but convict charge when only one specification
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not competent for a court-martial to find an accused not guilty of the specification, and yet guilty of the charge, where there is but one specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the court believes the accused is guilty of the charge but not precisely as laid in the specification, they should find him guilty of the latter with such exceptions or substitutions as may be necessary to present the facts as proved on the trial, and then guilty of the charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate and specific findings required
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be a separate and independent finding upon each charge and specification, and each separate finding should cover the charge or specification as to which it is made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If any charge or specification is proved only in part, the finding shall show specifically what is found to be proved and what not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court must decide legal sufficiency when plea splits
rubrics_metrics.description: When the accused pleads guilty to the specification and not guilty to the charge, the court is called upon to pass on the question of whether or not the specification sustains the charge as a matter of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the court so decides, it should find the accused guilty not only of the specification but of the charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to except and substitute in findings
rubrics_metrics.description: A court-martial is authorized to, in finding, except and substitute in a specification when any portion of the allegations is not proved, finding the accused guilty of a part of a specification only, excepting the remainder; or to substitute correct words or allegations in the place of such as are shown by the evidence to have been inserted through error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provided the exceptions or substitutions leave the specification still appropriate to the charge and legally sufficient thereunder, the court may properly find the accused guilty of the charge. Familiar instances include correcting erroneous name, rank, time, place, date, amount, quantity, quality, or other particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot except the gravamen while finding guilt on charge
rubrics_metrics.description: In finding guilty upon a specification, to except from such finding the word or words which express the gravamen of the act as charged and found is contradictory and irregular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Excepting the word 'fraudulent' in a finding while at the same time finding the accused guilty generally upon the charge of fraud is contradictory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding lesser included offenses by substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the evidence falls short of establishing a greater offense but shows a lesser included offense, the court may find the accused guilty of the lesser offense by excepting and substituting language in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Under a charge of desertion the court may, where appropriate, except 'did desert' and substitute 'did absent himself without authority,' then find on the charge 'not guilty, but guilty of absence without leave.' The findings on specification and charge should be consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible alternative finding: 'conduct to the prejudice of good order and military discipline'
rubrics_metrics.description: Where material allegations substantially made out do not fully sustain the charge as laid but clearly establish neglect of military duty or disorder in breach of military discipline, the accused may properly be found guilty of the specification and not guilty of the charge but guilty of 'conduct to the prejudice of good order and military discipline.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This form of finding is common where charge is laid under article 61; its legality is established in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on substitution across distinct specific articles
rubrics_metrics.description: The authority to substitute findings does not extend to finding a different specific offense under a charge laid under another specific article; such findings are irregular and invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: A court may not substitute a finding of larceny on a charge of burglary or find a violation of one specific article under a charge for another specific article; such findings are unauthorized and likely to be disapproved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge and superiority requirements for assault on superior officer
rubrics_metrics.description: To justify a conviction of a capital offense of offering violence against a superior officer under the twenty-first article of war it should be made to appear in evidence that the accused knew or believed that the person assaulted was in fact an officer in the Army and was his 'superior' in rank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mens rea element: accused must know/believe assaulted person was an officer and superior in rank.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officer assaulted must be 'in the execution of his office'
rubrics_metrics.description: Under a charge of a violation of article 21 in offering violence to a superior officer, it should be alleged and proved that the officer assaulted was at the time 'in the execution of his office.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof must show the officer was acting in his official capacity when assaulted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawfulness of order as element of disobedience charge
rubrics_metrics.description: Under a charge of a disobedience of the order of a superior officer in violation of article 21, it should be alleged, and should appear from the evidence introduced, that the order or 'command' was 'lawful.' An officer or soldier is not punishable under this article for disobeying an unlawful order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The order of a proper superior is presumed to be lawful and should be obeyed where not clearly and obviously in contravention of law. Unless illegality is unquestionable, one should obey first and seek redress afterwards; refusal based on opinion of unlawfulness is at the individual's risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for justified disobedience
rubrics_metrics.description: To justify, from a military point of view, a military inferior in disobeying the order of a superior, the order must be one requiring something to be done which is palpably a breach of law and a crime or an injury to a third person, or is of a serious character (not involving unimportant consequences only) and, if done, would not be susceptible of being righted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If not of this character, disobedience should not be justified and may be triable under another article (e.g., 62) if not triable under article 21. Emphasizes danger of permitting each soldier to determine for himself necessity or lawfulness of orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition/standard of drunkenness under Article 38
rubrics_metrics.description: The object of Article 38 is to enforce that measure of sobriety which is essential to the full and calm control of both the mental and physical faculties... Any intoxication which is sufficient to sensibly impair the rational and full exercise of the mental and physical faculties is drunkenness within the meaning of the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court should not attempt fine distinctions of degree (e.g., substituting 'under the influence' for 'drunk'); better to acquit than to create distinctions that defeat the article's purpose. It is not a sufficient defense to show that the accused, though under the influence of liquor, contrived to get through and somehow perform the duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sleeping on post: no defense from prior overtasking or poor discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: It is no defense to a charge of 'sleeping on post' that the accused had been previously overtasked by excessive guard duty, or that imperfect discipline prevailed in the command and similar offenses had been allowed to pass without notice, or that the accused was irregularly or informally posted as a sentinel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of such circumstances may, in general, be received in extenuation of the offense or to mitigate punishment after sentence. An officer who places or continues a soldier on duty as a sentinel when he is incompetent to perform duties from fatigue, infirmity, or other disability will ordinarily render himself liable to charges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restitution after the fact not a defense to Article 61
rubrics_metrics.description: It is no defense whatever to a charge under Article 61, that between the date of the refusal by the United States to pay the assignee of a duplicated voucher and the date of the arraignment... the money due has been paid, or somehow secured or made good to the assignees, or that he has been induced to withdraw or suspend his claim against the officer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Payment or settlement after the alleged offense does not negate criminal liability under Article 61.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleading distinguishing manslaughter from murder
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification alleging homicide, but not adding 'with malice aforethought,' or in terms to that effect, was pleading of manslaughter only and thus within Article 62.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form of allegation controls which article applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defense to embezzlement where loss without fault
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a defense to a charge under Article 62 of the embezzlement defined in section 5490, R.S., as consisting in a failure to safely keep public moneys by an officer charged with the safekeeping of the same, that the funds alleged to have been embezzled were, without fault on the part of the accused, lost in transportation or fraudulently or feloniously abstracted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accused may avoid liability if loss occurred without his fault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility and use of previous convictions for punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Executive order of March 30, 1898, previous convictions 'whatever their number within the prescribed period,' are admissible to aid the court in determining upon the proper measure of punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limits of punishment are operative only 'in time of peace'; in time of war, courts-martial are remitted to the discretion conferred by the Articles of War. Previous convictions may be considered to determine whether punishment limit is within or greater than an inferior court's power and to increase prescribed limit where authorized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on admissibility of prior convictions (enlistment/sentence approval)
rubrics_metrics.description: Previous convictions except of desertion on a trial for desertion, not adjudged during the current pending enlistment of the soldier but incurred during a prior enlistment, are not admissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of a previous conviction by a civil court is not admissible in this procedure. Evidence of a previous conviction is not admissible where the findings and sentence were disapproved by the proper reviewing authority; 'previous conviction' means a conviction to which effect has been given by approval of the sentence by competent authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility of prior convictions regardless of accused's failure to produce character testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: A court-martial refused to take into consideration evidence of previous convictions on grounds that the accused had been previously punished for each offense or had not introduced any testimony in support of his character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such objections were held not well taken; previous convictions may be considered for punishment even if accused has not offered character witnesses or was previously punished for same offenses (subject to other admissibility rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper documentary proof of previous convictions
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper evidence of a previous conviction is the record of the trial or a duly authenticated copy of the record or of the order of promulgation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copy of the summary court record should be certified by the post commander or adjutant to be a true copy. The certificate of the company commander is not a legal substitute. When the proof produced is the copy furnished the company or other commander it should be returned to him and a copy attached to the record of the general court-martial. The statement of service required by Army Regulations to be furnished the convening authority with general charges is not evidence of previous convictions.
